q.intro.text: Mathematicians made up a new number, i, with one rule: i squared is negative one. Everything else works like the algebra you already know.

q.ask.text: So what is two plus three i, times four plus i? Pick an answer, and say how sure you are.

e.intro.text: Four steps. Press each one: the picture moves first, then the algebra.

e.s0.text: Multiplying by i turns an arrow a quarter turn around zero: one turns into i. Turn again, and i times i lands on negative one. So i squared is negative one, and i sits off the real number line.

e.s1.text: Every term times every term, like any two binomials. Two times four is eight. Two times i is two i. Three i times four is twelve i. And three i times i is three i squared.

e.s2.text: Now the rule: i squared is negative one, so three i squared is three times negative one, which is negative three. That cell is a real number now.

e.s3.text: Collect real with real: eight minus three is five. Collect i with i: two i plus twelve i is fourteen i. So the product is five plus fourteen i.

e.why.text: Quick check. Why did the three i squared cell turn into negative three?

e.w-ok.text: Yes. i squared is negative one, so three i squared is negative three.

e.w-neg.text: If i were negative one, then i squared would be positive one. i is not negative one. It is the number whose square is negative one.

e.w-pos.text: Real squares are never negative, but i is not real. It was made so that i squared is negative one.

t.intro.text: Your turn: three minus two i, times one plus four i. The first two steps are done for you: i squared is negative one, and the box is filled.

t.i2.text: Step three. The corner cell holds negative eight i squared. Which real number is that?

t.i2-ok.text: Yes. Negative eight times negative one is eight. The cell turns real.

t.i2-plus.text: i squared is negative one, not positive one. Negative eight times negative one is positive eight.

t.i2-no.text: Replace i squared with negative one. Negative eight times negative one is what?

t.sum.text: Step four: collect, real with real and i with i. Type the product as a plus b i.

t.sum-ok.text: Yes. Three plus eight is eleven, and twelve i minus two i is ten i. The product is eleven plus ten i.

t.sum-plus.text: The corner cell is positive eight now, so the real part is three plus eight.

t.sum-sign.text: Mind the sign. Twelve i minus two i is ten i.

t.sum-mix.text: Keep the two kinds apart. The real cells are three and eight. The i cells are twelve i and negative two i.

t.cb-right.text: At the start you picked five plus fourteen i, and you were right. Now you can show why: every term times every term, then i squared is negative one.

t.cb-plus.text: At the start you picked eleven plus fourteen i. That treats i squared as positive one. The rule is i squared is negative one, so three i squared is negative three.

t.cb-fl.text: At the start you picked five. That multiplies only the firsts and the lasts. The cross terms, two i and twelve i, count too.

t.cb-none.text: Every term times every term, then i squared is negative one, then collect. That is how every complex product works.

p.intro.text: Sam says: the root of negative four, times the root of negative nine, is the root of thirty six, which is six, because root a times root b is the root of a times b. Is Sam right?

p.test.text: Let’s test it. Build the argument, and see where it leads.

p.build.text: Now prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.c1.text: Right. Each root of a negative is i times a real root. The root of negative four is two i.

p.c2.text: Right. The numbers multiply to six, and the two i’s are still there.

p.c3.text: Right. Six turns a quarter turn, then another. It lands on negative six, not six.

p.no.rule.text: That is Sam’s rule. It holds when a and b are not both negative. Here it gives the wrong answer.

p.no.neg.text: Negative two squared is four, not negative four. The principal root of negative four is two i.

p.no.ii.text: i times i is i squared, which is negative one. No i is left over.

p.no.other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line. Which reason makes this line true?

p.done.text: That’s a proof: three claims, each with its reason, and the plane backs every one. Write roots of negatives with i first. Root a times root b equals root a b fails when both are negative.
